I then led the implementation, and we launched two weeks later with idempotency protection in place.

results.question: Describe a performance problem you solved.
results.answer: At Northwind Logistics I added read replicas and query indexes to our tracking API, and p95 latency went from 900 milliseconds to 180.

sentences.text: At Northwind Logistics, I was a Backend Engineer owning our shipment-tracking APIs in Python and PostgreSQL that powered both customer tracking pages and driver apps.
We started getting complaints during peak hours because p95 latency had crept up to around 900 milliseconds and pages were timing out.
I dug into slow query logs and Postgres EXPLAIN plans and found two root causes: missing indexes on our hottest lookup queries, and our primary database getting saturated by read traffic.
I added targeted query indexes first and validated in staging that they fixed the worst queries without slowing down writes.
Then I added read replicas and split the traffic so all the heavy tracking reads went to the replicas while writes stayed on the primary.
I rolled it out gradually behind a config flag while watching replication lag closely to make sure tracking data stayed fresh.
As a result, p95 latency dropped from 900 milliseconds to 180 milliseconds, and timeouts essentially disappeared even during peak.
It also gave us headroom to scale without having to upsize the primary, which saved cost and a lot of on-call pain.

At Northwind Logistics, I was a backend engineer owning our shipment-tracking APIs in Python and Postgres.
We had a three-hour outage during peak shipping hours when a routine schema migration locked our primary tracking table.
I was on shift when support started reporting that tracking lookups were timing out, and I quickly confirmed our p95 latency had spiked and the database was queuing behind an exclusive lock.
I worked with the on-call DBA to kill the stuck migration, shift read traffic to our replicas to relieve pressure, and then carefully roll the migration back.
Once service recovered, I volunteered to write the full postmortem because I wanted us to actually learn from it.
I reconstructed the timeline, the missing lock-timeout guardrails, and why we'd run a blocking ALTER TABLE directly on a hot table with no dry run.
My core recommendations were to enforce statement and lock timeouts on all migrations, require concurrent index creation, and move to an expand-migrate-contract pattern for large tables.
We adopted those as team standards, added them to our runbook and CI checks, and we never had another migration-related outage while I was there.
It taught me to treat migrations as high-risk deploys and to always plan the rollback before I plan the rollout.

From that we put in place safer migration practices like adding lock timeouts, testing against production-like load, and running risky migrations off-peak with an explicit review checklist.
